Accrue

uh-KROO · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To accrue accumulate gradually (money).

Years of unused vacation days had quietly begun to accrue on the employee's account without her even realizing it.

Worked Example

The trust fund was designed so that the interest would accrue untouched for eighteen years, until the child turned into an adult and could finally access it.

Something gradually building up over time, bit by bit, until it becomes a significant total, is exactly what it means to accrue.

How Accrue Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

accumulate

accumulate: gradually gather or increase in amount

mount up

mount up: gradually increase to a large total

Antonyms

diminish

diminish: gradually become smaller

dwindle

dwindle: gradually decrease until very little is left

How Strong Is It? — add up → accrue → compound

add up vs. accrue

add up vs. accrue: Add up is a weaker, plainer term than accrue: loose coins add up in a jar, while interest that accrues builds steadily and more forcefully over time.

compound vs. accrue

compound vs. accrue: Compound is stronger than accrue: money that accrues grows steadily, but money that compounds grows ever faster, as earlier gains start earning gains of their own.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cre-/cru- (crescere)

root — cre-/cru- (crescere): to grow, to increase (Latin, via Old French acreue)

Put it together

Put it together: Accrue comes from Old French acreue, rooted in Latin crescere, 'to grow,' the same root behind crescent and increase. To accrue is to grow steadily, bit by bit, over time.

Use the root in a new word: crescent

Use the root in a new word: crescent: Through the telescope, the moon appeared as a thin, glowing crescent.
